dataset.name: Influence of hydrological, biogeochemical and temperature transients on subsurface carbon fluxes in a flood plain environment, Biogeochemistry: Dataset
description: To understand how reduced zones, water table fluctuations, and temperature gradients impact carbon exports from the Rifle floodplain system, we developed a biotic and abiotic reaction network and incorporated it into the reactive transport simulator TOUGHREACT. Two dimensional reactive flow and transport simulations were performed to: (1) quantify the release of carbon dioxide via abiotic processes, heterotrophic pathways, and autotrophic microbial oxidation of both reduced aqueous species (e.g., Fe+2, HS-) and minerals (e.g., pyrite), and (2) investigate the effects of reduced zones as well as water table variations and temperature gradients on subsurface carbon dynamics at the Rifle site.

This data package includes tables from Arora et al. 2016b: Influence of hydrological, biogeochemical and temperature transients on subsurface carbon fluxes in a flood plain environment. Biogeochemistry, 127(2-3), 367-396. In particular, files include reactive transport model parameters describing soil physical and thermal parameters, geochemical reaction network and rate laws, as well as initial and boundary conditions. The last table documents modeling results with respect to annual carbon fluxes from the site to the river.

spatialCoverage.description: Site: Rifle, Colorado US-RIF. The Rifle site is located in the east side of the Upper Colorado River Basin (UCRB) in northwestern Colorado. The site had a former uranium and vanadium mill, which operated between 1924 and 1958. As a uranium‐contaminated site it has been the focus of several intense hydrological, biogeochemical, and bioremediation research activities., and was used by the DOE Sustainable Systems Scientific Focus Area to explore how climate drivers influence hydrological processes and biogeochemical cycling within the Colorado River Basin. The Rifle site is located atop a floodplain adjacent to the Colorado River floodplain systems within the UCRB, and is representative of floodplains in the UCRB based upon its overall aquifer properties and hydrological coupling to the Colorado River.

Influence of hydrological, biogeochemical and temperature transients on subsurface carbon fluxes in a flood plain environment. Biogeochemistry, 127(2-3), pp.367-396.
measurementTechnique: To represent the geochemical system, the reactive transport code TOUGHREACT V3-OMP (Xu et al. 2011; Sonnenthal et al. 2014) was used. Several reactive transport simulations were run in which the degradation and oxidation of organic matter was simulated with increasing levels of complexity.

The simulations were divided into two categories—the first set of simulations (S1, S2 and S3) focused on steady water table and temperature conditions. One goal with these simulations was to obtain nearly steady chemical conditions that are generally representative of the field data (average pH, aqueous and gaseous concentrations, etc.) and result in the persistence of the NRZ near the TT-03 well location. The second set of simulations (S3.1 and S3.2) was restarted from the selected base case simulation (S3) to evaluate CO2 fluxes under seasonal water table variations (S3.1) and temperature gradients (S3.2).

TOUGHREACT was used together with the EOS9 equation of state module (Pruess et al. 1999) for isothermal simulations. The EOS9 module implements Richards’ equation (Richards 1931) for variably saturated flow of a single aqueous phase with air treated as a passive phase under conditions of constant pressure and temperature. Simulations considering variable temperature were run using the EOS3 module (Pruess et al. 1999), which simulates non-isothermal, multiphase (water, air) flow processes in variably saturated porous media.
